title: How Kleptomania Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss kleptomania, an impulse control disorder characterized by repeatedly failing to resist urges to steal items that are not needed or valuable, preceded by tension and relieved after theft. They open with holiday theft statistics from the Global Retail Theft Barometer, then cover the DSM criteria, a role-play of a kleptomaniac, hoarding cases (including a man in Israel), gender and demographics, the Ice Storm film, elderly shoplifting in Japan, legal defenses and the Justice Department's position, possible causes in brain research (serotonin transporter, frontal lobe, reward system), treatments (SSRIs, cognitive therapy, covert sensitization, aversion therapy, systematic desensitization, and a 2009 naltrexone study), and a brief history from St. Augustine and a 1816 Swiss physician's description. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about whether a man named Hippie Rob is the one a listener knew.

segments.title: Opening banter and holiday theft statistics
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about stealing season and cite the Global Retail Theft Barometer, which reported about 115 billion dollars in worldwide retail theft losses, with an 8.1 percent increase in North America.

segments.title: Defining kleptomania versus shoplifting
segments.summary: Chuck explains that kleptomania is not the same as shoplifting, which is only the means. He reads the DSM criteria: repeated failure to resist impulses to steal unneeded items, tension before theft, relief after, and no anger, revenge, delusion, or impaired judgment.

segments.title: Role-play of a kleptomaniac
segments.summary: Josh role-plays a kleptomaniac who pockets a lipstick tube, feels tension relieved by the theft, then guilt, and hides the item at his grandmother's house.

segments.title: Hoarding and the Israeli shoplifter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss hoarding of unused stolen goods, citing an early twentieth century upper-middle-class woman and a man in Israel who was caught in April with large amounts of unopened stolen merchandise after about a decade of shoplifting. His wife and son were suspected of knowing.

segments.title: Gender, age, and famous cases
segments.summary: They discuss that women are more often diagnosed with kleptomania, possibly because men who steal end up in prison and women less often admit it. Onset is usually in the early teens and twenties but can run to the late seventies. They mention The Ice Storm and elderly Japanese shoplifters, and a famous case of a woman who stole thousands from Sex Fifth Avenue.

segments.title: Legal defense and classification
segments.summary: A kleptomania defense is hard to prove because the defense must show no financial gain or revenge. The Justice Department does not recognize kleptomania as a defense. The hosts note it is classified as an impulse control disorder, possibly a symptom of other disorders, and that it is little studied because few kleptomaniacs are found.

segments.title: Brain research and causes
segments.summary: John Grant at the University of Minnesota studied the brain. Theories include a defect in a serotonin-transporting molecule, damage to frontal lobe circuits, reduced white matter, and involvement of the brain's reward system.

segments.title: Treatments and the 2009 naltrexone study
segments.summary: Treatments are hit or miss, with SSRIs sometimes working. Cognitive therapy, covert sensitization, aversion therapy, and systematic desensitization are described. A study begun in April gave naltrexone to 25 habitual thieves, and after eight weeks about two thirds of those on the drug had no urge to steal versus about eight percent on placebo.

segments.title: History of kleptomania
segments.summary: The hosts trace the history: the term appears in literature around the 3rd century CE with St. Augustine, then in 1816 a Swiss physician named Matthey described a madness of stealing without motive. Freud is mentioned, and the hosts note the shoplifting industry's dollar value.

segments.title: Listener mail: Hippie Rob
segments.summary: A listener writes about a man named Hippie Rob, and the hosts conclude he is probably not the same person, citing differences such as the missing dog, lack of alcohol aversion, and age. They invite further information by email.
